summary: Describes the format and syntax of a direction keyword used with bi-directional text in MIME, so mail can say whether text runs left to right or right to left.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes how MIME character-set names can indicate methods for displaying text that runs in different directions. It defines visual as the default and distinguishes implicit from explicit direction.

questions: how does mime indicate text direction
what do the -i and -e suffixes mean
subtitle: MIME character-set suffixes for visual, implicit, and explicit text direction.

tldr.problem: Arabic and Hebrew are read right to left and may appear alongside left-to-right text, while ordinary MIME character sets do not say how mixed-direction text should be presented.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes visual, implicit, and explicit direction methods and gives character-set examples using the suffixes -i and -e.
tldr.outcome: Visual direction is the default and requires no additional direction controls. The implicit and explicit methods rely on mechanisms described in ECMA TR/53.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1556 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a MIME convention for bidirectional text.

sections.title: The Mixed-Direction Text Problem
sections.content:
MIME can transport non-ASCII character sets such as Arabic ISO-8859-6 and Hebrew ISO-8859-8. These languages are read right to left, and a line may mix them with English text.

The memo describes character-set names that indicate whether the text uses implicit or explicit direction. The default remains visual direction using the previously defined ISO-8859 character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: A message may contain both right-to-left and left-to-right text. A display system needs to know which direction method the text expects.

sections.title: Three Presentation Methods
sections.content:
Visual direction displays all text according to the primary left-to-right display direction. The composing application must arrange the text so it displays correctly; the display application does not analyze its direction. This is the simplest method and the default for MIME text in this memo.

Implicit direction uses an algorithm based on character types and their positions. Explicit direction uses control sequences interleaved with the text. The RFC points implementers to ECMA TR/53 for the detailed rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Visual mode displays the prepared text as it is. Implicit mode works out direction from characters, while explicit mode marks direction with control codes.

sections.title: Character-Set Suffixes
sections.content:
The examples append -i for implicit mode and -e for explicit mode to character-set names. Examples include ISO-8859-6-i and ISO-8859-8-e.

The RFC says these names identify the direction method to use with the character data. Without either suffix, visual direction remains the default.
sections.plainLanguage: The suffix -i identifies implicit direction, and -e identifies explicit direction. With no suffix, the memo specifies visual direction.
